beats.intro: Lesson twenty-five. [[sub]]What a performance review is for, and how to judge performance fairly.
beats.asked: Grove asked a group of middle managers three questions. [[why]]Why do we review people? To assess, to improve, to motivate, to give feedback, to justify raises, and more. [[feel]]How do you feel giving one? Pride, anxiety, guilt, embarrassment, frustration. [[wrong]]And what was wrong with reviews you received? Too general. Mixed messages. No hint of how to improve. Negatives avoided. The boss didn't know my work. Only recent work counted. Surprises. [[hard]]Reviews are hard, and most managers don't do them well.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which complaint is it?
beats.purpose: Yet the review is the single most important form of task-relevant feedback a manager gives. [[rew]]It is also how rewards are handed out: promotions, money, stock. [[long]]And it shapes a person's performance for a long time, so it is one of your highest-leverage acts. [[one]]All the purposes are right, but one comes first: to improve the person's performance. [[skill]]That means two things. Find the missing skills, and fix them. [[mot]]And raise their motivation, so the same skills give more, like the higher curve in lesson twenty-one.
beats.judge: A review is the most formal kind of leadership. [[jury]]It is the only time you are required to act as judge and jury, and deliver the verdict face to face. [[prep]]Little prepares us for it. Our culture avoids confrontation. [[hung]]When Grove came from Hungary and said argument, people corrected him: you mean discussion. Talk about football or the weather, not anything that divides. [[size]]And reviews are not only for big companies. An insurance agent with two assistants needs them too. [[matters]]If performance matters, reviews are necessary.
beats.tight: First, assessing. [[obj]]Professional work has no cut-and-dried measure. Much of what people do this year shows up as output later, and only output is truly objective. [[rope]]So you walk a tightrope: be objective, but don't be afraid to use judgment. [[expect]]It helps to decide in advance what you expect, then judge against it. If you don't know what you want, you won't get it. [[okr]]Objectives help, but as lesson thirteen said, they are not a legal document.
beats.measures: Use the black box. [[out]]Output measures are what comes out: designs finished, sales quotas met, yield raised. Plot them on charts. [[int]]Internal measures are what goes on inside. Are we hitting this month's goals in a way that leaves people disgruntled in two months? Are we developing people for the future? [[weigh]]There is no formula for the weighting. It could be fifty-fifty, ninety-ten, or ten-ninety, and it can shift. [[know]]But know which two things you are trading off.
beats.longshort: A similar trade-off: the long term against the short. [[eng]]An engineer must finish a product on a strict schedule, to bring in revenue. [[method]]He is also building a design method that will help others design similar products later. [[pv]]Both deserve review. To weigh them, borrow present value from finance: what will the future work pay back, and what is that worth today?
beats.q2: Quick check. Output or internal measure?
beats.offset: Then there is a time offset between activity and output. Grove learned it the hard way. [[good]]One of his managers had a superb year. Sales up, good margins, products working. [[straw]]But turnover was high and people grumbled. Grove gave him a very positive review anyway. [[dive]]The next year the group took a nose dive. [[stars]]Grove concluded the manager had actually improved in year two. The great results were work from a year before, like light from distant stars. [[wrong]]The superior rating had been wrong. He should have trusted the internal measures. [[other]]It works the other way too. Someone building a factory from scratch had no output yet, and Grove gave him credit. [[judge]]Your job is to judge performance, not just record it.
beats.potential: When you review a manager, judge both the person and the group. [[add]]Ask what value they add: hiring, training, anything that improves the team's future output. [[trap]]And avoid the potential trap. Assess performance, not potential: substance, not form. [[gm]]Grove was asked to approve a high rating for a general manager whose unit lost money, missed forecasts, and slipped schedules. His boss said: but he is an outstanding manager. It was his organization that did badly. [[cap]]Grove refused. A manager's rating cannot be higher than the rating of his organization. [[signal]]Otherwise the message is: act like a good manager. You don't need to perform like one.
beats.promote: Promotions follow reviews, and nothing shows your values more loudly than who you promote. [[role]]Each one becomes a role model. [[sales]]The old saying goes: promote your best salesman and you lose a good salesman and gain a bad manager. [[worst]]But should the worst salesman get the job? Promoting the best says performance counts. [[better]]And however well someone did, you can always suggest how to do better. With hindsight, compare what they did with what they might have done.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]The review's main purpose is to improve performance: skills and motivation. [[w2]]You are judge and jury: decide what you expect in advance. [[w3]]Weigh output and internal measures, now and later. [[w4]]Watch the time offset: judge performance, don't just record it. [[w5]]Rate performance, not potential, and promote it. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson twenty-five.
